topics.title: Hormone synthesis, receptors and signalling
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 1 Principles of Endocrinology; Ch. 2 Principles of Hormone Action

mustKnow.fact: Peptide hormones act through cell-surface receptors, while steroid hormones and thyroid hormone act mainly through nuclear receptors. Thyroid hormone must also enter the cell through a transporter such as MCT8.

An activating GNAS variant causes McCune-Albright syndrome, with fibrous dysplasia, cafe-au-lait macules, and autonomous endocrine hyperfunction. A maternally inherited inactivating GNAS variant causes pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a, with Albright hereditary osteodystrophy and resistance to PTH. The same skeletal picture without hormone resistance, pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, follows paternal inheritance because GNAS is imprinted.

Pulsatile GnRH stimulates LH and FSH, whereas continuous GnRH receptor stimulation desensitizes the axis. That is why a pulsatile pump can induce fertility and a long-acting GnRH agonist suppresses puberty or hormone-dependent disease.

Cortisol follows a diurnal rhythm, highest in the early morning and lowest around midnight. Loss of that rhythm is a clue to Cushing syndrome, which is why a midnight salivary cortisol is used and a random afternoon cortisol is not a screening test.

Only the free hormone fraction is active. Estrogen raises thyroid-binding globulin and sex hormone-binding globulin, so total thyroxine rises in pregnancy while a euthyroid woman remains euthyroid. Androgens lower sex hormone-binding globulin.
Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome is an MCT8 mutation. T3 cannot enter neurons normally, so affected boys have severe neurodevelopmental delay with a high serum T3 and a low or normal T4.

Apparent mineralocorticoid excess occurs when 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 fails to inactivate cortisol to cortisone in the kidney. Cortisol then activates the mineralocorticoid receptor. Licorice inhibits the same enzyme.

Spare receptors mean a maximal response can occur when only a fraction of receptors are occupied. A fall in receptor number then shifts the dose needed for a half-maximal response before it lowers the maximum response, which is the usual pattern of moderate insulin resistance.

topics.title: Endocrine testing and assay interpretation
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 4 Laboratory Techniques for Recognition of Endocrine Disorders; Ch. 6 Pituitary Physiology and Diagnostic Evaluation

mustKnow.fact: Biotin interferes with streptavidin-based immunoassays. Sandwich assays such as TSH read falsely low, and competitive assays such as free T4 read falsely high, which can imitate Graves disease. Stop biotin for at least 48 hours before these blood tests.

The hook effect is a falsely low reading when the analyte is extremely high, classically a giant prolactinoma. Serial dilution unmasks the true prolactin. Heterophile antibodies do the opposite and can falsely raise a sandwich assay.

Macroprolactin is a biologically quiet prolactin-immunoglobulin complex. Polyethylene glycol precipitation that leaves a recovery below 40% means macroprolactin accounts for most of the measured prolactin, and treatment is not required for that finding alone.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society hyperprolactinemia guidance; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: The insulin tolerance test is the reference stimulation test for cortisol and growth hormone reserve. It is adequate only if glucose falls below 40 mg/dL. It is contraindicated in ischemic heart disease, seizure disorder, and frail older adults.

A peak growth hormone at or below 5.1 mcg/L on an adequate insulin tolerance test supports adult growth hormone deficiency using the Endocrine Society cutoff. The glucagon test is the usual alternative when hypoglycemia is unsafe, and obesity lowers the peak that counts as deficient.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society evaluation of adult growth hormone deficiency

mustKnow.fact: The 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is a screen, not a localization test. A next-morning cortisol of 1.8 mcg/dL (50 nmol/L) or higher is an abnormal result. Do not image the pituitary or the adrenals before the biochemical diagnosis is secure.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline 2008; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling separates pituitary Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH secretion. A central to peripheral ACTH ratio of at least 2 before CRH, or at least 3 after CRH, supports a pituitary source. It is done only after ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome is proved.

Adrenal vein sampling is a localization test for primary aldosteronism after the diagnosis is confirmed and surgery is desired. With cosyntropin, a selectivity index of at least 5 shows the catheter is in the adrenal vein, and a lateralization index of at least 4 supports a unilateral source.

topics.title: Hypopituitarism and pituitary apoplexy
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 6 Pituitary Physiology and Diagnostic Evaluation; Ch. 7 Pituitary Adenomas and Masses

mustKnow.fact: Replace cortisol before thyroxine in suspected hypopituitarism. Starting levothyroxine while cortisol is low can precipitate an adrenal crisis because thyroid hormone speeds cortisol clearance.

In slowly progressive hypopituitarism, growth hormone and gonadotropins usually fail before TSH and ACTH. Apoplexy and hypophysitis break that order, and ACTH deficiency can be the first and most dangerous deficit.
Sheehan syndrome follows severe postpartum hemorrhage. Failure to lactate and persistent amenorrhea are the classic clues, and other anterior pituitary deficits can appear later.

Pituitary apoplexy presents with sudden severe headache, visual loss, and acute cortisol deficiency, often into an existing adenoma. Give intravenous hydrocortisone as soon as the diagnosis is suspected. Surgery is for deteriorating vision or a falling level of consciousness, not for every bleed.

Lymphocytic hypophysitis often presents in late pregnancy or after delivery. ACTH deficiency is common, the stalk may be thickened, and it can imitate a pituitary mass. Hormone replacement is required even when the mass is observed.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor hypophysitis is linked more strongly to CTLA-4 blockade than to PD-1 blockade. ACTH deficiency is often permanent. High-dose glucocorticoid treats mass effect but does not reliably restore pituitary function.
mustKnow.source: Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 44 The Immunoendocrinopathy Syndromes

mustKnow.fact: Adult growth hormone replacement is considered only after other deficient axes are replaced and a stimulation test confirms the deficit. It is not started on a low IGF-1 alone. The insulin tolerance test cutoff used by the Endocrine Society is a peak at or below 5.1 mcg/L.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society evaluation of adult growth hormone deficiency

mustKnow.fact: Traumatic brain injury and subarachnoid hemorrhage can cause hypopituitarism at the time of injury or months later. An empty sella is often an incidental imaging finding and does not by itself prove hormone deficiency.

topics.title: Hyperprolactinaemia and prolactinoma
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 7 Pituitary Adenomas and Masses; Endocrine Society hyperprolactinemia guidance

mustKnow.fact: A prolactinoma is the most common functioning pituitary adenoma. Mild hyperprolactinemia also comes from drugs, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, and stalk compression. A prolactin below 200 ng/mL with a large mass is more consistent with stalk effect than with a macroprolactinoma, whereas a level in the thousands favors a prolactinoma.

Cabergoline is first-line drug therapy for a prolactinoma because it normalizes prolactin and shrinks the tumor more reliably than bromocriptine. Transsphenoidal surgery is for dopamine agonist resistance or intolerance, apoplexy with vision loss, a cerebrospinal fluid leak, or a patient who prefers surgery for a circumscribed microadenoma.
Check an echocardiogram when cabergoline is used above 2 mg per week for a prolonged period, because of the risk of valvular regurgitation. Most prolactinoma doses are below that threshold.

Before treating a mildly raised prolactin, exclude macroprolactin and the hook effect. The hook effect makes a giant prolactinoma look like a nonfunctioning mass with only a modest prolactin, and dilution reveals the true value.

In a microprolactinoma, stop the dopamine agonist once pregnancy is confirmed. If a drug must be continued for a macroadenoma that threatens vision, bromocriptine has the longer pregnancy safety record. Monitor visual fields if a macroadenoma is present.

Antipsychotics, especially risperidone, and metoclopramide raise prolactin by dopamine blockade. Do not start a dopamine agonist for drug-induced hyperprolactinemia without talking to the prescribing clinician, because it can worsen psychosis.

Dopamine agonist resistance means prolactin does not normalize or the tumor does not shrink meaningfully. The next step is a higher cabergoline dose in selected patients, or surgery, not an automatic switch to radiotherapy.

A prolactinoma can present with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, infertility, or hypogonadism in a man, including reduced libido and a low testosterone that will not correct until the prolactin falls. Always measure prolactin in a sellar mass before labeling it nonfunctioning.

topics.title: Acromegaly and gigantism
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 6 Pituitary Physiology and Diagnostic Evaluation; Ch. 7 Pituitary Adenomas and Masses

mustKnow.fact: Screen for acromegaly with an age-adjusted IGF-1. A random growth hormone does not diagnose or exclude the disease. Confirm with an oral glucose tolerance test: failure of the growth hormone nadir to fall below 1 mcg/L supports the diagnosis, and some sensitive assays use a nadir below 0.4 mcg/L.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society acromegaly guideline 2014; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 6

mustKnow.fact: Transsphenoidal surgery is first-line treatment for most resectable somatotroph adenomas. A biochemical cure is a normal age-adjusted IGF-1 and a random growth hormone below 1 mcg/L.

Long-acting somatostatin analogues, octreotide LAR and lanreotide, are used when surgery does not cure the disease. Pasireotide can control residual disease but often worsens hyperglycemia. Pegvisomant, a growth hormone receptor antagonist, lowers IGF-1 while the measured growth hormone rises, so IGF-1 is the marker, and liver enzymes and tumor size must be watched.
Acromegaly causes cardiomyopathy, sleep apnea, insulin resistance, carpal tunnel syndrome, and colonic neoplasia. Colonoscopy is indicated at diagnosis.

Gigantism is growth hormone excess before the epiphyses close. Very early childhood gigantism suggests X-linked acrogigantism from GPR101 duplication. Familial isolated pituitary adenoma often involves AIP, and those tumors present younger and respond less well to somatostatin analogues.

McCune-Albright syndrome and Carney complex are syndromic causes of growth hormone excess. Carney complex includes spotty skin pigmentation, cardiac myxomas, and primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease, with PRKAR1A variants.

Headache, sweating, enlarging hands and feet, and a change in ring or shoe size are the clinical clues. A normal IGF-1 makes active acromegaly unlikely and is the right test when the question is whether a suggestive face is the disease.

Diabetes or hypertension that is hard to control in a patient with acral enlargement should trigger an IGF-1, not a random growth hormone. Residual disease after surgery is tracked with IGF-1, not with tumor size alone.

topics.title: Cushing syndrome
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 13 The Adrenal Cortex; Ch. 7 Pituitary Adenomas and Masses; Endocrine Society Cushing syndrome guideline 2008

mustKnow.fact: Screen for Cushing syndrome with late-night salivary cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or the 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test. Two abnormal results support the diagnosis when the clinical suspicion is real. A morning cortisol of 1.8 mcg/dL or higher after 1 mg dexamethasone is abnormal.

Once Cushing syndrome is confirmed, measure plasma ACTH. A value below 10 pg/mL favors an ACTH-independent adrenal source. A value above 20 pg/mL favors an ACTH-dependent source, either a pituitary adenoma or ectopic secretion. Values between those cutoffs are repeated.

Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is the most accurate test to separate Cushing disease from ectopic ACTH secretion when the pituitary MRI is negative or equivocal. A central to peripheral ACTH ratio of at least 3 after CRH supports a pituitary source.

Do not order a pituitary MRI or an adrenal CT as the first test for suspected Cushing syndrome. Nonfunctioning incidentalomas are common, and imaging is interpreted only after biochemistry shows where the cortisol is coming from.

Alcohol excess, severe depression, and poorly controlled diabetes can cause pseudo-Cushing physiology and an abnormal suppression test. The history is part of the test, and a single abnormal screen is not an operation.

First-line treatment of Cushing disease is transsphenoidal surgery. When surgery is not curative, options include repeat surgery, radiotherapy, or medical therapy. Ketoconazole, metyrapone, and osilodrostat block cortisol synthesis. Osilodrostat inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase.

Mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor. Serum cortisol rises or stays high and cannot be used to judge control, so glucose and clinical features are followed instead. Pasireotide can treat Cushing disease but worsens hyperglycemia.

Nelson syndrome is an enlarging corticotroph tumor with rising ACTH and skin pigmentation after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing disease. Subclinical autonomous cortisol secretion is a failed 1 mg dexamethasone test without overt Cushing stigmata, usually from an adrenal incidentaloma, and it is linked to hypertension, diabetes, and bone loss.

modules.name: Nonfunctioning pituitary adenomas and sellar masses

topics.title: Nonfunctioning pituitary adenomas and sellar masses
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 7 Pituitary Adenomas and Masses

mustKnow.fact: A microadenoma is smaller than 10 mm and a macroadenoma is 10 mm or larger. Every sellar incidentaloma needs a prolactin and an IGF-1. Test for cortisol excess when the clinical picture suggests it or the mass is a macroadenoma. Check visual fields if the mass approaches the chiasm.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society pituitary incidentaloma guideline 2011; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 7

mustKnow.fact: Most clinically nonfunctioning adenomas are gonadotroph tumors. They present with mass effect: headache, bitemporal hemianopia, or hypopituitarism. Surgery is indicated when vision is compressed or a macroadenoma is growing. A stable microincidentaloma does not need an operation.
Always exclude a prolactinoma with a diluted prolactin before calling a giant sellar mass nonfunctioning. A dopamine agonist, not surgery, is first-line treatment if the mass is a macroprolactinoma.

Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma is the childhood form, often calcified and cystic, and is driven by CTNNB1. Papillary craniopharyngioma is the adult form and often carries BRAF V600E. Both can cause hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus, and hypothalamic obesity.
A Rathke cleft cyst is a benign remnant that can mimic a cystic adenoma. It is usually observed unless it compresses the chiasm or causes hormone deficiency.

Hypophysitis, from lymphocytic disease, IgG4 disease, or CTLA-4 blockade, thickens the stalk and often presents with ACTH deficiency rather than hormone excess. It is a medical mass, not an automatic surgical one.

After transsphenoidal surgery, watch for cortisol deficiency, for the triphasic water disturbance of early diabetes insipidus, then hyponatremia, then possible permanent diabetes insipidus, and for cerebrospinal fluid leak.
Pituitary carcinoma is defined by metastasis, not by histology of the sellar mass. Temozolomide is used for aggressive pituitary tumors and carcinomas that progress after surgery and radiotherapy.

topics.title: Arginine vasopressin deficiency and resistance
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 8 Posterior Pituitary

mustKnow.fact: Arginine vasopressin deficiency, also called central diabetes insipidus, and arginine vasopressin resistance, also called nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, both produce large volumes of dilute urine. Primary polydipsia produces dilute urine too, but the plasma is usually slightly dilute and the urine concentrates when water is withheld.

In the water deprivation test, diabetes insipidus fails to concentrate the urine above about 300 mOsm/kg while plasma osmolality rises above 295 mOsm/kg. Desmopressin then raises urine osmolality by more than 50% in arginine vasopressin deficiency and does not do so in resistance.

After hypertonic saline, a copeptin of 4.9 pmol/L or lower indicates arginine vasopressin deficiency. A baseline copeptin of 21.4 pmol/L or higher indicates arginine vasopressin resistance and can avoid a deprivation test.
mustKnow.source: NEJM 2018 copeptin after hypertonic saline; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 8

mustKnow.fact: Desmopressin is the treatment for arginine vasopressin deficiency. Too much desmopressin causes hyponatremia. Adipsic diabetes insipidus, usually after hypothalamic injury, is dangerous because thirst does not protect the sodium, so fluid intake is prescribed.

Lithium is the classic cause of arginine vasopressin resistance. Amiloride is the preferred diuretic because it blocks lithium entry through the epithelial sodium channel. Thiazides and a low-solute diet reduce urine volume when resistance is from other causes.

After pituitary surgery the water balance can be triphasic: early diabetes insipidus, then a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis as stored vasopressin leaks, then permanent diabetes insipidus if the neurons were destroyed. A sodium that falls in the second phase is treated by stopping desmopressin and restricting water, not by giving more desmopressin.
Pregnancy can unmask arginine vasopressin deficiency because placental vasopressinase breaks down vasopressin. Desmopressin is resistant to that enzyme and is the drug used in pregnancy.

The plasma sodium is often normal in diabetes insipidus if the person can drink freely. A high sodium means access to water is impaired or thirst is broken. Polyuria with a low-normal sodium suggests primary polydipsia until the deprivation test or copeptin says otherwise.

modules.name: SIADH and disorders of water balance

topics.title: SIADH and disorders of water balance
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 8 Posterior Pituitary

mustKnow.fact: The syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis causes hypotonic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine, urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg, urine sodium usually above 30 mmol/L, and clinical euvolemia. Thyroid, adrenal, and renal failure must be excluded before the label is used.
Common causes are small cell lung cancer, pneumonia, subarachnoid hemorrhage, carbamazepine, SSRIs, and cyclophosphamide. A chest radiograph is part of a new unexplained case in a smoker.

Fluid restriction is first-line treatment for mild asymptomatic hyponatremia from this syndrome. Severe symptoms, including seizures or deep drowsiness, are treated with hypertonic 3% saline, often as a 100 mL bolus, while the cause is addressed.
mustKnow.source: European and American hyponatremia guidance; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 8

mustKnow.fact: In patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination, including sodium below 120 mmol/L, alcohol use, malnutrition, and liver disease, limit the rise in sodium to 8 mmol/L in 24 hours. A rise up to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours is the usual ceiling when that risk is lower.
mustKnow.source: Hyponatremia correction guidance; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 8

mustKnow.fact: Tolvaptan, a vasopressin antagonist, is an option for resistant euvolemic hyponatremia in hospital. Do not combine it with hypertonic saline. Overcorrection is the hazard, so the sodium is checked often.

Cerebral salt wasting is hypovolemic hyponatremia after brain injury, with a high urine sodium. It is treated with saline replacement, not fluid restriction. Calling it SIADH and restricting water makes the volume loss worse.
Secondary adrenal insufficiency and severe hypothyroidism can imitate the laboratory picture of SIADH. A low morning cortisol must be treated before the hyponatremia is blamed on a lung cancer alone.

Reset osmostat is a stable mild hyponatremia in which the urine dilutes once the sodium falls a little further. It does not need aggressive correction. The diagnosis is one of exclusion after volume status and cortisol are reviewed.

topics.title: Thyroid physiology and function tests
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 9 Thyroid Pathophysiology and Diagnostic Evaluation

mustKnow.fact: TSH is the screening test for thyroid function in a person with an intact pituitary. In pituitary disease the TSH is unreliable, and free T4 is the test that shows central hypothyroidism.

The Wolff-Chaikoff effect is a transient block of thyroid organification after an iodine load, followed by escape. The Jod-Basedow effect is iodine-induced thyrotoxicosis in a nodular gland or latent Graves disease, and escape does not protect those patients.

Most circulating T3 comes from peripheral conversion of T4 by deiodinases. Nonthyroidal illness raises reverse T3 and lowers T3, with a low or normal free T4 and a TSH that is normal or transiently low. Do not start levothyroxine for those labs during an acute illness unless thyroid disease was already likely.
mustKnow.source: Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 9; Ch. 48 Endocrine Disorders of Critical Illness

mustKnow.fact: Estrogen and pregnancy raise thyroid-binding globulin, so total T4 rises while the free fraction stays normal in a euthyroid woman. Androgens, nephrotic syndrome, and severe liver disease lower thyroid-binding globulin and the total T4.
The circulating half-life of T4 is about 7 days and that of T3 is about 1 day. That is why a missed levothyroxine dose is not an immediate crisis and why liothyronine wears off quickly.

Biotin can imitate thyrotoxicosis on the laboratory report, with a low TSH and a high free T4, while the patient is clinically euthyroid. Stop biotin for at least 48 hours and repeat the test before treating.
mustKnow.source: ATA laboratory guidance; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 4

mustKnow.fact: A suppressed TSH with a normal free T4 and free T3 is subclinical thyrotoxicosis. A TSH below 0.1 mIU/L in an older adult, or in a patient with atrial fibrillation or osteoporosis, is usually treated. A mildly low TSH in a young asymptomatic person can be observed.

Amiodarone is iodine rich and also inhibits T4 to T3 conversion. It can cause either hypothyroidism or thyrotoxicosis, so a baseline TSH is checked and symptoms are not blamed on the heart drug without a repeat TSH and free T4.

topics.title: Hypothyroidism
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 11 Hypothyroidism and Thyroiditis

mustKnow.fact: Primary hypothyroidism has a high TSH and a low free T4. Subclinical hypothyroidism has a high TSH and a normal free T4. Hashimoto thyroiditis is the usual cause where iodine intake is sufficient, and TPO antibodies support that cause.

Full replacement levothyroxine in a young adult is about 1.6 mcg/kg/day, taken fasting and separated from calcium, iron, and some antacids. In older adults and in known coronary disease, start at 25 to 50 mcg and titrate to the TSH.
mustKnow.source: ATA hypothyroidism guidance; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 11

mustKnow.fact: Treat subclinical hypothyroidism when the TSH is 10 mIU/L or higher. Below that, treat if the patient is pregnant, trying to conceive, or clearly symptomatic, especially if TPO antibodies are positive. A TSH that is only slightly high in a frail older adult often does not need replacement.
Central hypothyroidism has a low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH. Titrate levothyroxine to the free T4, not the TSH, and replace cortisol first if hypopituitarism is possible.

Myxedema coma is decompensated hypothyroidism with hypothermia, hyponatremia, hypoventilation, and a precipitant such as infection or a sedative. Give intravenous levothyroxine, a typical load of 200 to 400 mcg, plus glucocorticoid until adrenal insufficiency is excluded, and use passive rewarming.

In pregnancy, increase the levothyroxine dose by about 30% as soon as conception is suspected, which is 2 extra tablets a week, and check the TSH about every 4 weeks. Return to the pre-pregnancy dose after delivery.

Levothyroxine requirements rise with estrogen, with drugs that induce its metabolism such as rifampin, carbamazepine, and phenytoin, and with malabsorption or coeliac disease. A rising TSH on a stable dose should prompt a review of how and when the tablet is taken.
Do not treat nonthyroidal illness with levothyroxine. A low T3 in a patient in the intensive care unit is an adaptation, not myxedema, unless the history and the free T4 show true hypothyroidism.
mustKnow.source: Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 48 Endocrine Disorders of Critical Illness

topics.title: Graves disease and thyrotoxicosis
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 10 Hyperthyroid Disorders; ATA hyperthyroidism guideline

mustKnow.fact: Graves disease causes diffuse thyrotoxicosis with a high radioiodine uptake, TSH-receptor antibodies, and sometimes orbitopathy or pretibial myxedema. A toxic nodule or toxic multinodular goiter has focal or patchy uptake and no TSH-receptor antibodies.

Painless thyroiditis, iodine exposure, and exogenous thyroid hormone all suppress uptake. Factitious thyrotoxicosis has a low thyroglobulin, whereas thyroiditis has a high thyroglobulin. Antithyroid drugs do not treat thyroiditis.

Methimazole is the preferred antithyroid drug except in the first trimester of pregnancy and in thyroid storm, when propylthiouracil is preferred. Propylthiouracil also blocks peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, but it can cause severe liver injury, so it is not long-term first-line therapy.

Agranulocytosis from an antithyroid drug presents with fever and sore throat. Stop the drug and do not restart either thionamide, because the reaction can cross. Routine blood counts do not replace that warning.

Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy and during breastfeeding. It can worsen thyroid eye disease, so active moderate or severe orbitopathy is a reason to choose surgery or an antithyroid drug instead, or to cover radioiodine with glucocorticoid if it must be used in milder active disease.

A beta blocker, often propranolol, is started for symptomatic thyrotoxicosis because it relieves adrenergic symptoms and propranolol also slows T4 to T3 conversion. It does not treat the underlying gland.

Thyroid storm is a clinical diagnosis. A Burch-Wartofsky score of 45 or higher is highly suggestive. Treat with a thionamide first, propylthiouracil if it is available, then iodine, a beta blocker, and glucocorticoid, and treat the precipitant. Never give iodine before the thionamide.
mustKnow.source: ATA hyperthyroidism guideline; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 10

mustKnow.fact: Subclinical hyperthyroidism with a TSH below 0.1 mIU/L is treated in patients older than about 65 years and in those with heart disease or osteoporosis. Beta blockade alone is not enough when the TSH stays fully suppressed and the risk is high.

topics.title: Thyroiditis
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 11 Hypothyroidism and Thyroiditis

mustKnow.fact: Subacute thyroiditis, also called de Quervain thyroiditis, follows a viral illness with a very painful gland, a high ESR, thyrotoxicosis, and a near-absent radioiodine uptake. Treat pain with an NSAID or a glucocorticoid and symptoms with a beta blocker. Antithyroid drugs are not indicated.

The usual course of subacute, silent, and postpartum thyroiditis is thyrotoxicosis, then hypothyroidism, then recovery. The hypothyroid phase may need temporary levothyroxine. A minority remain permanently hypothyroid.

Silent thyroiditis and postpartum thyroiditis are painless, often TPO-antibody positive, and have low radioiodine uptake. Postpartum thyroiditis occurs in the first year after delivery and is more likely if TPO antibodies were positive in pregnancy.

Acute suppurative thyroiditis is a bacterial infection with fever and a tender gland, usually in a euthyroid patient, sometimes from a pyriform sinus fistula on the left in a child. Treatment is antibiotics and drainage, not an antithyroid drug.

Riedel thyroiditis is a hard, fixed, IgG4-related gland that can cause compressive symptoms and hypoparathyroidism. It is not a cancer, although the clinical feel imitates one, and the diagnosis is histologic.

Amiodarone type 1 thyrotoxicosis is iodine-induced hyperthyroidism in a nodular or Graves gland, with measurable vascularity, and is treated with a thionamide. Type 2 is a destructive thyroiditis with absent Doppler flow and is treated with glucocorticoid. Mixed disease occurs.

Hashitoxicosis is a transient thyrotoxic phase of Hashimoto thyroiditis. Uptake is low or variable and TPO antibodies are high. It is not treated as Graves disease with a prolonged course of methimazole unless TSH-receptor antibodies and high uptake show true Graves disease.

Do not give radioiodine or a thionamide for the thyrotoxic phase of subacute thyroiditis. The gland is not making new hormone in excess; it is leaking stored hormone, and iodine or an antithyroid drug does not stop that leak.

topics.title: Thyroid nodules and thyroid cancer
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 12 Nontoxic Diffuse Goiter, Nodular Thyroid Disorders, and Thyroid Malignancies; ATA differentiated thyroid cancer guideline 2015

mustKnow.fact: Measure TSH first in a thyroid nodule. If the TSH is low, do a radionuclide scan. A hot autonomous nodule is rarely malignant and is not biopsied. A cold or warm nodule, or any nodule when the TSH is not suppressed, is considered for fine-needle aspiration based on sonographic risk and size.

Bethesda categories run from I nondiagnostic and II benign through III atypia of undetermined significance, IV follicular neoplasm, V suspicious for malignancy, and VI malignant. A follicular carcinoma cannot be diagnosed on cytology because capsular or vascular invasion is a histologic finding.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma is the common differentiated cancer. Nuclear grooves, orphan Annie nuclei, and psammoma bodies are the classic histology, spread is usually lymphatic, and BRAF V600E is the common driver. Prognosis is excellent for intrathyroidal disease in a young adult.
Follicular thyroid carcinoma spreads by blood to bone and lung rather than to nodes. Hurthle cell carcinoma is the oncocytic variant and takes up radioiodine less reliably.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from C cells, secretes calcitonin and CEA, and shows amyloid that stains with Congo red. It does not concentrate radioiodine. Measure metanephrines before thyroidectomy because it may be the first sign of MEN2, and a pheochromocytoma must be treated first.
mustKnow.source: ATA medullary thyroid cancer guidance; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 12

mustKnow.fact: The ATA does not recommend a serum calcitonin on every thyroid nodule. Calcitonin is measured when medullary carcinoma is suspected, when cytology is suggestive, or when a family history of MEN2 is present.

Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is a disease of older adults, with a rapidly enlarging hard mass and airway compromise. Test for BRAF V600E, because a BRAF-directed combination can change an otherwise very poor course. It is staged as stage IV at diagnosis.

After treatment of differentiated thyroid cancer, follow thyroglobulin and thyroglobulin antibody, not TSH alone. Radioiodine remnant ablation is not mandatory for low-risk intrathyroidal papillary carcinoma. TSH suppression is tighter for high-risk disease than for low-risk disease that is in remission.

topics.title: Thyroid disease in pregnancy
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 19 Endocrine Changes in Pregnancy; Ch. 9 Thyroid Pathophysiology and Diagnostic Evaluation; ATA thyroid in pregnancy 2017

mustKnow.fact: If a trimester-specific TSH reference range is not available, the ATA accepts an upper limit of about 4.0 mIU/L. The lower limit in the first trimester can be about 0.1 mIU/L because hCG stimulates the thyroid.
A woman already on levothyroxine should increase the dose by about 30%, 2 extra tablets a week, as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, and have the TSH checked about every 4 weeks through mid pregnancy.

Use propylthiouracil in the first trimester because methimazole is associated with aplasia cutis and choanal atresia. After the first trimester many clinicians switch back to methimazole because propylthiouracil hepatotoxicity is the greater ongoing risk. Both drugs cross the placenta.

Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis from very high hCG, often with hyperemesis, has a suppressed TSH, a negative TSH-receptor antibody, and no goiter or orbitopathy. It is not treated with an antithyroid drug. Graves disease in pregnancy has a positive TSH-receptor antibody.

TSH-receptor antibody crosses the placenta and can cause fetal and neonatal thyrotoxicosis. Measure it at the first visit in a woman with current or past Graves disease, including after definitive therapy with radioiodine or surgery.
Radioiodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. A pregnancy test is confirmed before radioiodine in any person who could be pregnant.
The WHO iodine intake in pregnancy is 250 mcg per day. Severe iodine deficiency causes maternal and fetal hypothyroidism and is still a preventable cause of impaired neurodevelopment.
mustKnow.source: WHO iodine requirement; ATA thyroid in pregnancy 2017

mustKnow.fact: Postpartum thyroiditis occurs within 12 months of delivery, often with a thyrotoxic phase then a hypothyroid phase, a low uptake, and positive TPO antibodies. The thyrotoxic phase is managed with a beta blocker, not methimazole. A TSH is checked at about 6 weeks if the woman is symptomatic.

topics.title: Thyroid eye disease
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 10 Hyperthyroid Disorders; EUGOGO thyroid eye disease guideline 2021

mustKnow.fact: Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune orbitopathy of Graves disease, driven in part by the TSH receptor and the IGF-1 receptor on orbital fibroblasts. Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor and must be stopped.

Activity is scored with the clinical activity score. A score of 3 or higher out of 7 means active disease. Severity is mild, moderate to severe, or sight-threatening. Sight-threatening disease means dysthyroid optic neuropathy or corneal breakdown.

Lid lag and stare can occur in any thyrotoxicosis. Proptosis, restrictive strabismus, and inflammatory soft-tissue signs point to thyroid eye disease itself. The inferior rectus is the muscle most often involved.
For mild active thyroid eye disease, selenium 100 mcg twice daily for 6 months improves outcomes in selenium-insufficient populations, together with lubricants and smoking cessation.

For moderate to severe active disease, a standard course is intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg weekly for 6 weeks and then 250 mg weekly for 6 weeks. The cumulative glucocorticoid dose should stay below 8 g because higher doses raise the risk of severe liver injury.

Teprotumumab, an IGF-1 receptor inhibitor, is used for moderate to severe thyroid eye disease and reduces proptosis. Hyperglycemia is an important adverse effect, especially in a patient who already has diabetes.

Sight-threatening dysthyroid optic neuropathy is treated urgently with high-dose intravenous glucocorticoid. If vision does not respond, urgent orbital decompression is required. This is not a clinic follow-up in a month.

Radioiodine can worsen active thyroid eye disease. Euthyroidism should be restored and kept stable, because both hypothyroidism and ongoing hyperthyroidism aggravate the orbit. Glucocorticoid cover is used if radioiodine is given to a patient with risk factors for progression.

topics.title: Adrenal insufficiency
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 13 The Adrenal Cortex; Endocrine Society adrenal insufficiency guideline 2016

mustKnow.fact: Primary adrenal insufficiency has a low cortisol and a high ACTH, with hyperpigmentation, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and a high renin because mineralocorticoid is also lost. Secondary adrenal insufficiency has a low or inappropriately normal ACTH, no hyperpigmentation, and a preserved mineralocorticoid axis, so potassium is usually normal.

A standard 250 mcg cosyntropin test that fails to raise cortisol to 18 mcg/dL (500 nmol/L) at 30 or 60 minutes diagnoses adrenal insufficiency on older polyclonal assays. Newer specific assays use a lower cutoff near 14 to 15 mcg/dL, so the laboratory cutoff must be read with the result. The test does not distinguish primary from secondary disease in the first weeks after pituitary injury.

A morning cortisol below 3 mcg/dL strongly suggests adrenal insufficiency. A morning cortisol above 15 mcg/dL makes it unlikely if the patient is not acutely ill. Values in between need a stimulation test.

Do not delay hydrocortisone to perform a cosyntropin test in suspected adrenal crisis. Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately and infuse saline. A typical ongoing crisis dose is 50 mg every 6 hours or a continuous infusion, then taper to oral therapy.

Chronic primary adrenal insufficiency is replaced with hydrocortisone about 15 to 25 mg a day in two or three doses, the largest in the morning, plus fludrocortisone, usually 50 to 200 mcg a day. Fludrocortisone is not given for secondary adrenal insufficiency.

Sick-day rules double or triple the oral glucocorticoid for fever or illness, and parenteral hydrocortisone is used if the patient is vomiting. Every patient needs a supply they can inject and a steroid card.

Autoimmune adrenalitis, confirmed with 21-hydroxylase antibodies, is the common cause where tuberculosis is rare. In India, tuberculosis remains an important cause and can calcify the adrenals. Other causes include hemorrhage, metastases, and drugs such as ketoconazole, mitotane, and etomidate, which blocks 11-beta-hydroxylase.

Checkpoint inhibitor therapy can cause primary adrenalitis. A new hyponatremia with hypotension on immunotherapy is adrenal crisis until proved otherwise, and hydrocortisone comes before the confirmatory labs are back.
mustKnow.source: Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 44 The Immunoendocrinopathy Syndromes

topics.title: Primary aldosteronism and mineralocorticoid excess
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 14 Endocrine Hypertension; Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism guideline 2016

mustKnow.fact: Screen for primary aldosteronism in resistant hypertension, hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalemia, an adrenal incidentaloma with hypertension, early-onset hypertension, or a family history of early hypertension or stroke. Many patients are normokalemic, so a normal potassium does not exclude the disease.

The screening test is the plasma aldosterone concentration divided by plasma renin. A commonly used positive screen is a ratio above 30 when aldosterone is measured in ng/dL and renin in ng/mL/h, together with an aldosterone above 10 ng/dL. The laboratory's own cutoff and units must be used.

Stop spironolactone and eplerenone for 4 to 6 weeks before the ratio, because they raise renin and can falsely normalize the screen. A beta blocker can suppress renin and falsely raise the ratio, so an abnormal result on a beta blocker still needs confirmation.

Confirm with a suppression test unless spontaneous hypokalemia, undetectable renin, and a plasma aldosterone above 20 ng/dL already make the diagnosis obvious. After intravenous saline, failure of aldosterone to fall below 10 ng/dL supports primary aldosteronism. Saline loading is avoided in uncontrolled hypertension or heart failure.

A unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma, Conn syndrome, is treated by laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Bilateral idiopathic hyperplasia is treated with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Spironolactone causes gynecomastia; eplerenone is the alternative.

Adrenal vein sampling is recommended before surgery in most patients who want an operation. It can be omitted in a patient younger than 35 years with marked aldosterone excess, spontaneous hypokalemia, and a clear unilateral adenoma with a normal contralateral gland on imaging.

Familial hyperaldosteronism type I, glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism, is a chimeric CYP11B1/CYP11B2 gene. Aldosterone is under ACTH control, so low-dose dexamethasone suppresses it, and family members are screened. It presents with early hypertension and hemorrhagic stroke.

Do not start a workup for primary aldosteronism by removing an incidental adrenal nodule. Imaging cannot tell a nonfunctioning adenoma from an aldosterone-producing one. Biochemistry and, when needed, adrenal vein sampling come first.

topics.title: Pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 14 Endocrine Hypertension; Endocrine Society pheochromocytoma guideline 2014

mustKnow.fact: The classic triad is headache, palpitations, and sweating, with paroxysmal or sustained hypertension, but many patients have only hypertension. Screen with plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines, drawn under quiet conditions. Metanephrines are preferred over catecholamines because the tumor secretes them continuously.

A metanephrine result more than 3 times the upper limit is highly suggestive. Mild elevations are often false positives from tricyclic antidepressants, SNRIs, physical stress, or an upright draw. Confirm before any imaging or biopsy.

Image only after biochemistry is positive. Start with CT or MRI of the abdomen and pelvis. Use Ga-68 DOTATATE or another functional scan when the mass is extra-adrenal, metastatic, or not found on CT. Never biopsy a suspected pheochromocytoma.

At least 30% of pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas carry a germline pathogenic variant. The main syndromes are MEN2 (RET), von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, and the SDH genes. SDHB carries the highest risk of metastatic extra-adrenal disease.

Prepare every patient with alpha blockade before surgery, usually for 7 to 14 days, with phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin, a high-salt diet, and volume replacement. Add a beta blocker only after alpha blockade if tachycardia persists. A beta blocker first leaves alpha stimulation unopposed and can cause a crisis.
After the tumor is removed, watch for hypotension and for hypoglycemia from rebound insulin release. Postoperative glucose checks are part of recovery, not an optional extra.

In pregnancy, phenoxybenzamine is the usual alpha blocker. If the diagnosis is made early, surgery is planned in the second trimester. A crisis at term is managed with blockade and delivery in a center that can anesthetize a blocked patient.

Metastatic disease is more likely with an extra-adrenal paraganglioma and an SDHB variant. Options include radionuclide therapy, chemotherapy, and tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Blood pressure control with alpha blockade continues even when the tumor cannot be removed.

topics.title: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 13 The Adrenal Cortex; Endocrine Society congenital adrenal hyperplasia guideline 2018

mustKnow.fact: 21-hydroxylase deficiency is the common form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Cortisol is low, ACTH is high, and adrenal androgens are high. Salt-wasting disease also lacks aldosterone. A markedly elevated 17-hydroxyprogesterone, often above 10000 ng/dL in classic disease, makes the diagnosis.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society congenital adrenal hyperplasia guideline 2018

mustKnow.fact: Nonclassic 21-hydroxylase deficiency can imitate polycystic ovary syndrome. A cosyntropin-stimulated 17-hydroxyprogesterone above 1000 ng/dL supports nonclassic disease. Measure it when hyperandrogenism is atypical, early, or familial.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society congenital adrenal hyperplasia guideline 2018

mustKnow.fact: A virilized newborn needs an urgent 17-hydroxyprogesterone, electrolytes, and a karyotype. Salt-wasting crisis, with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and shock, typically appears in the first 1 to 4 weeks, not on the first day of life.

Growing children with classic disease are treated with hydrocortisone, not with long-acting glucocorticoid, because dexamethasone suppresses growth. Fludrocortisone and sodium chloride supplements are added in the salt-wasting form. Doses are raised for illness.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society congenital adrenal hyperplasia guideline 2018

mustKnow.fact: 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency causes virilization plus hypertension and hypokalemia, because 11-deoxycortisol and deoxycorticosterone build up. 17-hydroxyprogesterone can be mildly high, but 11-deoxycortisol is the marker that separates it from 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency blocks sex-steroid and cortisol synthesis and raises deoxycorticosterone. The picture is hypertension, hypokalemia, and absent puberty, with a 46,XY infant who looks undervirilized or a 46,XX adolescent who does not develop secondary sexual characteristics.

3-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency raises DHEA and can cause ambiguous genitalia in both 46,XX and 46,XY infants, with salt wasting in severe disease. It is rare compared with 21-hydroxylase deficiency.

Prenatal dexamethasone to prevent virilization of an affected female fetus is not routine care, because the exposed unaffected fetuses take a risk for an uncertain benefit. Genetic counseling is the standard, not empiric early steroid.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society congenital adrenal hyperplasia guideline 2018

topics.title: Adrenal incidentaloma and adrenocortical carcinoma
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 13 The Adrenal Cortex; European Society of Endocrinology adrenal incidentaloma guideline

mustKnow.fact: Every adrenal incidentaloma needs a 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, even if the patient is not Cushingoid. Screen metanephrines if hypertension or spells are present, and measure the aldosterone-renin ratio if hypertension or unexplained hypokalemia is present.
mustKnow.source: European Society of Endocrinology adrenal incidentaloma guideline

mustKnow.fact: On an unenhanced CT, an attenuation below 10 Hounsfield units means a lipid-rich adenoma and is benign imaging. Higher attenuation needs washout or another technique. Absolute washout above 60% and relative washout above 40% support a benign adenoma.
mustKnow.source: European Society of Endocrinology adrenal incidentaloma guideline

mustKnow.fact: The risk of adrenocortical carcinoma rises with size. Surgery is considered for a mass of 4 cm or larger that is not a clear benign adenoma, for any hormone excess that needs an operation, and for suspicious imaging such as irregular margins or rapid growth.
mustKnow.source: European Society of Endocrinology adrenal incidentaloma guideline

mustKnow.fact: Do not biopsy an adrenal mass until a pheochromocytoma has been excluded biochemically, and do not biopsy a typical adenoma at all. Biopsy is for a patient with a known extra-adrenal cancer when the result would change treatment.
mustKnow.source: European Society of Endocrinology adrenal incidentaloma guideline

mustKnow.fact: Autonomous cortisol secretion is a failed 1 mg dexamethasone test without overt Cushing syndrome. It is associated with hypertension, diabetes, and osteoporosis, and the decision for surgery is individualized rather than automatic.
mustKnow.source: European Society of Endocrinology adrenal incidentaloma guideline

mustKnow.fact: Adrenocortical carcinoma often co-secretes cortisol and androgens, so virilization plus Cushing features in a large adrenal mass is carcinoma until proved otherwise. A pure aldosterone-secreting carcinoma is uncommon.

Mitotane is the adrenolytic drug used for adrenocortical carcinoma. It induces cortisol metabolism and can cause adrenal insufficiency, so glucocorticoid replacement is given with it and levels are followed. ENSAT staging and the Ki-67 index guide prognosis.

A clearly benign nonfunctioning adenoma under 4 cm does not need years of repeated CT. One follow-up image is enough if the first study was indeterminate, and hormone testing is repeated only if new clinical features appear.
mustKnow.source: European Society of Endocrinology adrenal incidentaloma guideline

topics.title: Hypercalcaemia and primary hyperparathyroidism
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 27 Hormones and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism

mustKnow.fact: Correct the calcium for albumin: add about 0.8 mg/dL for each 1 g/dL that albumin is below 4 g/dL. Then interpret PTH. A high or inappropriately normal PTH with hypercalcemia is PTH-dependent. A suppressed PTH is PTH-independent.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is usually a single adenoma, about 85% of cases, less often four-gland hyperplasia, and rarely carcinoma. Hyperplasia is the pattern in MEN1. Carcinoma is suspected when calcium is very high, a mass is palpable, or PTH is extreme.

Surgery is indicated for symptomatic disease, including stones and fragility fractures, and for asymptomatic disease when calcium is more than 1 mg/dL above the upper limit, age is under 50 years, eGFR is below 60, T-score is -2.5 or lower, there is a vertebral fracture, or 24-hour urine calcium is above 400 mg with increased stone risk.
mustKnow.source: Fourth International Workshop on asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism

mustKnow.fact: Localize with ultrasound or sestamibi only after the decision to operate. A negative scan does not exclude the diagnosis, and imaging is not a diagnostic test. Four-gland disease will not be cured by removing one hot spot.

Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is an inactivating CASR variant with lifelong mild hypercalcemia, a normal or mildly high PTH, and a calcium to creatinine clearance ratio below 0.01. Parathyroidectomy does not cure it and should not be done.

Hypercalcemia of malignancy with a suppressed PTH is usually PTHrP from squamous, renal, or breast cancer, local osteolysis from myeloma, or calcitriol from lymphoma. Ectopic PTH is rare. The first treatment of severe hypercalcemia is intravenous saline, then a bisphosphonate, with calcitonin as a short bridge.

Glucocorticoid lowers calcium when the cause is calcitriol excess, as in lymphoma and granulomatous disease. It does not treat primary hyperparathyroidism. Milk-alkali syndrome causes hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and renal impairment with a suppressed PTH.

Hungry bone syndrome after parathyroidectomy causes hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and hypomagnesemia as the skeleton takes mineral back up. Calcium and calcitriol are given, and magnesium is replaced, until the bones settle.

topics.title: Hypocalcaemia and hypoparathyroidism
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 27 Hormones and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism

mustKnow.fact: Hypocalcemia causes neuromuscular irritability, a prolonged QT interval, and, when severe, seizures or laryngospasm. Trousseau sign is more specific than Chvostek sign. The ECG is checked before calcium is given intravenously.

A low calcium with a low or inappropriately normal PTH is hypoparathyroidism. A low calcium with a high PTH is secondary hyperparathyroidism from vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, or chronic kidney disease, or it is PTH resistance.

The common acquired cause is neck surgery. Magnesium deficiency causes functional hypoparathyroidism and must be corrected or calcium will not stay up. Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism is part of APS-1 when candidiasis and adrenal insufficiency are also present.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a, from a maternal GNAS variant, has Albright hereditary osteodystrophy plus resistance to PTH, so PTH is high, calcium is low, and phosphate is high. TSH resistance is common. Paternal inheritance of the same skeletal picture without hormone resistance is pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism.

Acute symptomatic hypocalcemia is treated with intravenous calcium gluconate on a cardiac monitor, after magnesium is checked. Give 1 to 2 g of calcium gluconate and repeat as needed. Do not put calcium into a line that contains bicarbonate.

Chronic hypoparathyroidism is treated with calcium and calcitriol, aiming for a low-normal serum calcium so that urine calcium does not stay high. Thiazides can reduce hypercalciuria. Recombinant PTH is reserved for patients who cannot be controlled without hypercalciuria or who need very large doses.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society hypoparathyroidism guidance; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 27

mustKnow.fact: Activating CASR variants cause autosomal dominant hypocalcemia, with a low PTH and a tendency to hypercalciuria. Pushing the serum calcium into the normal range with calcitriol can cause nephrocalcinosis, so the target is a little below normal.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism is not treated by removing parathyroid tissue. The glands are responding correctly to a receptor defect. Give calcium and active vitamin D, and replace the other resistant axes, especially TSH.

topics.title: Vitamin D, rickets and osteomalacia
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 27 Hormones and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism; Ch. 30 Rickets and Osteomalacia

mustKnow.fact: 25-hydroxyvitamin D is the storage form used to judge vitamin D status. The IOM defines deficiency as below 20 ng/mL. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is not a screening test: it can be normal or high in deficiency because PTH drives the 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
mustKnow.source: IOM dietary reference intake for vitamin D; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 27

mustKnow.fact: An older Endocrine Society target of 30 ng/mL is not required for the general population, and the 2024 guideline moved away from routine screening of healthy adults. Deficiency treatment is still indicated when 25-hydroxyvitamin D is low and bone disease, malabsorption, or a drug such as an enzyme-inducing anticonvulsant is present. NICE and the IOM agree that population screening of asymptomatic adults is not useful.
mustKnow.source: Endocrine Society vitamin D guideline 2024; IOM

mustKnow.fact: Nutritional rickets and osteomalacia show a low or low-normal calcium, a low phosphate, a high PTH, a high alkaline phosphatase, and a low 25-hydroxyvitamin D. Children have rachitic rosary and widened wrists. Adults have bone pain, proximal weakness, and Looser zones.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 1 is 1-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency from CYP27B1. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is low and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is normal. Treatment is calcitriol, not cholecalciferol alone.

Vitamin D-dependent rickets type 2 is vitamin D receptor resistance. 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is very high, and many patients have alopecia. Ordinary vitamin D replacement does not correct the receptor defect.

X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets is a PHEX variant that raises FGF23. Phosphate is wasted, calcium and PTH are typically normal at presentation, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is low or inappropriately normal. Burosumab, an FGF23 antibody, is disease-modifying treatment. Phosphate plus calcitriol is the older regimen.

Tumor-induced osteomalacia is an acquired FGF23 syndrome from a small mesenchymal tumor. Biochemistry matches hypophosphatemic rickets in an adult who was previously well. Ga-68 DOTATATE is used to find the tumor, and removal cures the phosphate wasting.

Chronic kidney disease lowers 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D because of lost 1-alpha-hydroxylase, raises FGF23 and PTH, and lowers phosphate excretion. Give active vitamin D or a vitamin D analogue for secondary hyperparathyroidism, not high-dose cholecalciferol alone, once the GFR is very low.

topics.title: Osteoporosis
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 29 Osteoporosis: Basic and Clinical Aspects

mustKnow.fact: A T-score of -2.5 or lower at the lumbar spine, total hip, or femoral neck in a postmenopausal woman or a man aged 50 or older is osteoporosis. A fragility fracture of the hip or vertebra is osteoporosis even when the T-score is better than -2.5. A Z-score of -2.0 or lower in a younger adult prompts a search for a secondary cause.
mustKnow.source: WHO densitometry definition; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 29

mustKnow.fact: The NOF treatment thresholds often quoted for osteopenia are a 10-year hip fracture probability of at least 3% or a major osteoporotic fracture probability of at least 20% on FRAX. These are United States thresholds, not a universal Indian cutoff.

Before treating, look for secondary causes: hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, hypogonadism, Cushing syndrome, coeliac disease, myeloma, aromatase inhibitors, and glucocorticoid use. A low Z-score makes that search mandatory.

Oral alendronate and yearly intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg are first-line antiresorptive drugs. Take oral bisphosphonates fasting with water and stay upright. Atypical femoral fracture and osteonecrosis of the jaw are uncommon at osteoporosis doses and much more a concern at the high doses used in cancer.
mustKnow.source: AACE/ACE postmenopausal osteoporosis guideline; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 29

mustKnow.fact: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months is an antiresorptive option when bisphosphonates cannot be used. Stopping it without a follow-on bisphosphonate causes rapid bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures. Do not start it unless the next dose and the exit plan are clear.

Teriparatide and abaloparatide are anabolic agents for very high fracture risk. The teriparatide course is limited, historically to 24 months, and an antiresorptive drug follows so the new bone is kept. Romosozumab is given for 12 months and then followed by an antiresorptive. It carries a cardiovascular caution and is avoided after myocardial infarction or stroke.

For glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, the ACR treats patients starting prednisone at 2.5 mg or more daily for an expected 3 months or longer when fracture risk is moderate or high. High-risk patients start a bisphosphonate or an anabolic drug with the steroid, not after the first fracture.

Calcium intake of about 1000 to 1200 mg elemental calcium a day from diet plus supplement, and correction of vitamin D deficiency, are the background of every regimen. Calcium alone does not treat established osteoporosis with a fracture.

modules.name: Paget disease and other metabolic bone disorders

topics.title: Paget disease and other metabolic bone disorders
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 27 Hormones and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism; Ch. 29 Osteoporosis: Basic and Clinical Aspects

mustKnow.fact: Paget disease of bone is focal high turnover. Alkaline phosphatase is high, calcium and phosphate are usually normal, and a radionuclide bone scan shows the extent. The radiograph may show a blade-of-grass lesion in a long bone or a cotton-wool skull.

A single infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg is first-line treatment when Paget disease needs therapy. Treat symptomatic disease, disease at a site where a complication is likely such as the skull base or a weight-bearing bone, and pagetic bone that is about to be operated on.

Complications of Paget disease include deafness, osteoarthritis, fracture, high-output heart failure when the disease is extensive, and, rarely, osteosarcoma. A new mass or a change in pain pattern needs imaging for sarcoma.
Osteitis fibrosa cystica, the brown tumor of severe primary hyperparathyroidism, is not Paget disease. Calcium and PTH are high in osteitis fibrosa and are normal in uncomplicated Paget disease.

Osteogenesis imperfecta from COL1A1 or COL1A2 causes brittle bones, and the classic severe and mild forms include blue sclerae, hearing loss, and sometimes dentinogenesis imperfecta. A child with recurrent fractures and normal calcium needs this diagnosis considered before a label of non-accidental injury is the only thought.

Fibrous dysplasia is a mosaic GNAS disease. The shepherd's crook deformity of the proximal femur is characteristic. In McCune-Albright syndrome it occurs with cafe-au-lait macules and autonomous endocrine function.

Osteopetrosis is overly dense bone that fractures and can compress cranial nerves. The malignant infantile form causes bone marrow failure. Carbonic anhydrase II deficiency adds renal tubular acidosis to the dense bones.

Sclerostin deficiency, as in sclerosteosis and van Buchem disease, causes very high bone mass. Romosozumab blocks sclerostin to treat osteoporosis and is a different clinical use of the same pathway, given for 12 months and followed by an antiresorptive drug.

modules.name: Diagnosis, classification and pathogenesis of diabetes

topics.title: Diagnosis, classification and pathogenesis of diabetes
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 33 Pathophysiology of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; ADA Standards of Care 2025

mustKnow.fact: Diabetes is diagnosed by a fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, a 2-hour OGTT value of 200 mg/dL or higher, an HbA1c of 6.5% or higher, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms. Without symptoms, a second test confirms the first unless the glucose is unequivocally high.
Prediabetes is a fasting glucose of 100 to 125 mg/dL, a 2-hour glucose of 140 to 199 mg/dL, or an HbA1c of 5.7% to 6.4%. These bands are ADA definitions and are not yet diabetes.

Type 1 diabetes is immune beta-cell destruction. GAD65, IA-2, ZnT8, and insulin autoantibodies support the diagnosis, and C-peptide is low once the honeymoon ends. Adult-onset antibody-positive disease is latent autoimmune diabetes of adults and often needs insulin within months to a few years.
mustKnow.source: ADA Standards of Care 2025; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 35

mustKnow.fact: In the Diabetes Prevention Program, lifestyle change reduced progression from impaired glucose tolerance to diabetes by 58%, and metformin reduced it by 31%. Lifestyle was more effective in older adults, and metformin was most useful in younger adults with a higher BMI.
mustKnow.source: Diabetes Prevention Program; ADA Standards of Care 2025

mustKnow.fact: Teplizumab, given as a 14-day course in stage 2 type 1 diabetes (multiple autoantibodies plus dysglycemia, but not yet insulin-requiring), delays the onset of stage 3 clinical diabetes. It does not replace insulin once clinical diabetes is present.
mustKnow.source: ADA Standards of Care 2025; TN-10 trial

mustKnow.fact: Ketosis-prone type 2 diabetes presents with diabetic ketoacidosis, often in a person of African or Asian ancestry, with negative islet antibodies, and then remits so that insulin can be stopped. It is not classic type 1 diabetes.

Fibrocalculous pancreatic diabetes is seen in tropical regions including India. A young lean patient has pancreatic calcification, abdominal pain, and insulin-requiring diabetes that is often not ketosis prone. Look at the pancreatic film before labeling every young adult as type 1.

Type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell failure. The ominous octet describes extra defects, including increased glucagon, increased hepatic glucose production, and incretin deficiency. Fasting glucose reflects hepatic glucose output more than muscle uptake.

modules.name: Type 1 diabetes, insulin therapy and technology

topics.title: Type 1 diabetes, insulin therapy and technology
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 35 Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus; Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 36 Digitized Approaches to Diabetes Diagnostics and Therapeutics

mustKnow.fact: Physiologic insulin replacement in type 1 diabetes is basal plus bolus. A typical total daily dose is 0.4 to 1.0 units/kg. On a sick day the basal insulin is never stopped, ketones are checked, and extra rapid-acting insulin is given, with carbohydrate if glucose is falling.

The DCCT showed that intensive insulin therapy reduced retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy compared with conventional therapy. The EDIC follow-up showed that the microvascular benefit persisted after the HbA1c difference narrowed, which is the legacy effect. Weight gain and severe hypoglycemia were the costs.
mustKnow.source: DCCT and EDIC; Williams Endocrinology 15e Ch. 35

mustKnow.fact: CGM targets for most adults are time in range 70 to 180 mg/dL above 70% of readings, time below 70 mg/dL under 4%, and time below 54 mg/dL under 1%. Time above 180 mg/dL should be under 25%.

Insulin degludec lasts beyond 42 hours and is still dosed once daily. Once-weekly insulin icodec is a weekly basal option studied in the ONWARDS trials. Rapid analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) cover meals; they do not replace basal insulin.

Automated insulin delivery, a pump plus CGM that adjusts basal insulin, reduces hypoglycemia compared with injections in type 1 diabetes. Carbohydrate counting is still required for most hybrid closed-loop systems because the meal bolus is announced.
The honeymoon phase is partial remission after diagnosis, with a falling insulin requirement. It ends. Stopping insulin completely during the honeymoon risks ketoacidosis and is not advised.

Islet transplantation is considered for selected adults with type 1 diabetes and severe hypoglycemia unawareness or marked glycemic lability that technology has not fixed. Immunosuppression is the trade-off, so it is not first-line therapy.

Lipodystrophy and erratic absorption follow repeated injections into the same site. Rotate sites. A rising insulin requirement with hard lumps at the injection sites is a technique problem before it is a new diagnosis.

topics.title: Pharmacotherapy of type 2 diabetes
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 34 Therapeutics of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; ADA and EASD consensus

mustKnow.fact: Metformin remains usual first-line therapy when the eGFR is at least 30 mL/min and it is tolerated. Do not start it if the eGFR is below 45 in many labels' caution band, and stop it if the eGFR is below 30. Long-term use is associated with vitamin B12 deficiency, so B12 is checked if anemia or neuropathy appears.

When atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease is present, an SGLT2 inhibitor or a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven benefit is added independent of HbA1c. Metformin alone is not sufficient risk-reduction therapy in those patients.
mustKnow.source: ADA and EASD consensus; ADA Standards of Care 2025

mustKnow.fact: SGLT2 inhibitors cause genital mycotic infection, volume depletion, and euglycemic ketoacidosis. Hold them when a patient is acutely ill or not eating, and stop them about 3 days before planned surgery. A near-normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis on these drugs.

GLP-1 receptor agonists lower glucose and weight and can cause nausea. They carry a boxed warning for medullary thyroid carcinoma based on rodent C-cell tumors, so they are avoided in MEN2 and in personal medullary carcinoma. Do not combine a GLP-1 receptor agonist with a DPP-4 inhibitor.

Sulfonylureas lower glucose but cause hypoglycemia and weight gain. Glyburide is a poor choice when the eGFR is low because active metabolites accumulate. DPP-4 inhibitors are weight neutral and do not cause hypoglycemia by themselves. Saxagliptin was linked to heart failure hospitalization in SAVOR-TIMI 53 and is avoided in heart failure.
Pioglitazone improves insulin resistance but causes fluid retention and is contraindicated in heart failure. It also raises fracture risk. It is not a drug for a patient who is already edematous.

The usual HbA1c target is below 7% for most nonpregnant adults. A tighter target below 6.5% is only for selected patients who can reach it without hypoglycemia. A target near 8% is appropriate when life expectancy is limited or hypoglycemia risk is high. The ACCORD trial, which pushed HbA1c below 6% in longstanding type 2 diabetes with high cardiovascular risk, increased mortality.

Start basal insulin when the patient is catabolic, when HbA1c is very high with symptoms, or when oral therapy including a GLP-1 receptor agonist is not enough. A common start is 10 units or 0.1 to 0.2 units/kg at bedtime, titrated to the fasting glucose. The UKPDS legacy effect means early glycemic control still matters years later.

modules.name: Cardiovascular and renal outcome trials in diabetes

topics.title: Cardiovascular and renal outcome trials in diabetes
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 34 Therapeutics of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus; ADA Standards of Care 2025

mustKnow.fact: EMPA-REG OUTCOME showed that empagliflozin reduced three-point major adverse cardiovascular events, cardiovascular death, and hospitalization for heart failure in type 2 diabetes with established cardiovascular disease.
mustKnow.source: EMPA-REG OUTCOME; ADA Standards of Care 2025

mustKnow.fact: CANVAS showed that canagliflozin reduced major adverse cardiovascular events. It also reported a higher amputation rate that later SGLT2 inhibitor trials did not establish as a class effect. Foot risk is still assessed before the drug is chosen.

DECLARE-TIMI 58 showed that dapagliflozin was noninferior for major adverse cardiovascular events and reduced hospitalization for heart failure, in a population that included many people without prior cardiovascular disease.

LEADER showed that liraglutide reduced three-point major adverse cardiovascular events. SUSTAIN-6 showed that injectable semaglutide also reduced those events and was associated with a retinopathy signal, so a recent rapid fall in glucose and existing retinopathy are reviewed before it is started.

REWIND showed that dulaglutide reduced major adverse cardiovascular events in a population in which most participants did not have established cardiovascular disease. GLP-1 receptor agonist benefit is not limited to secondary prevention.

CREDENCE showed that canagliflozin reduced kidney failure and cardiovascular events in type 2 diabetes with albuminuric chronic kidney disease. DAPA-CKD and EMPA-KIDNEY extended SGLT2 inhibitor kidney benefit to chronic kidney disease with or without diabetes.

FIDELIO-DKD showed that finerenone, a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, reduced a kidney composite in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease already on renin-angiotensin blockade. FIGARO-DKD showed a reduction in cardiovascular events. Hyperkalemia is the adverse effect to monitor.

SELECT showed that semaglutide 2.4 mg reduced major adverse cardiovascular events in people with overweight or obesity and cardiovascular disease who did not have diabetes. FLOW showed that semaglutide reduced progression of kidney disease in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease.

topics.title: Diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar state
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 35 Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus; ADA diabetic ketoacidosis consensus

mustKnow.fact: Diabetic ketoacidosis is hyperglycemia, usually a glucose above 250 mg/dL, with an arterial pH below 7.3, a bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L, and ketonemia. Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the ketone to measure. Urine nitroprusside does not detect beta-hydroxybutyrate well.

Fluids come first. Start intravenous insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour after potassium is known. If the serum potassium is below 3.3 mmol/L, hold insulin and replace potassium first, because insulin will drive potassium into cells and can stop the heart.

Add dextrose when glucose falls to about 200 mg/dL and continue insulin until the anion gap closes. Give potassium in the fluids when the serum potassium is between 3.3 and 5.2 mmol/L. Bicarbonate is reserved for a pH below 6.9.

Resolution requires a closed anion gap, a bicarbonate of at least 18 mmol/L, a pH above 7.3, and the ability to eat. Overlap subcutaneous insulin with the intravenous infusion by 1 to 2 hours so ketoacidosis does not rebound. Basal insulin can be started earlier in the admission.

Cerebral edema is mainly a complication of diabetic ketoacidosis in children and adolescents and is associated with a too-rapid fall in osmolality. Treat with mannitol or hypertonic saline and slow the fluid correction. It is not routine in adult hyperosmolar coma.

Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state has a glucose often above 600 mg/dL, effective osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, pH above 7.3, bicarbonate above 18 mmol/L, and little ketonemia, with altered sensorium. The fluid deficit is larger than in ketoacidosis. Insulin is started after fluids, often at 0.05 units/kg/hour if glucose is falling with saline alone.

Effective osmolality is calculated as 2 times sodium plus glucose in mg/dL divided by 18. Urea is omitted because it is freely permeable. A falling osmolality is the target, not a normal glucose in the first hour.

SGLT2 inhibitors cause euglycemic ketoacidosis, with glucose that may be below 200 mg/dL and a high anion gap from beta-hydroxybutyrate. Treat with insulin and dextrose together, and stop the SGLT2 inhibitor. Do not send the patient home because the glucose is only 160 mg/dL.

topics.title: Hypoglycaemia
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 39 Hypoglycemia; Endocrine Society hypoglycemia evaluation guideline 2009

mustKnow.fact: Whipple triad is symptoms of hypoglycemia, a low measured plasma glucose, and relief of symptoms when glucose is raised. A fingerstick alone, without the triad, does not diagnose an insulinoma.

ADA level 1 hypoglycemia is a glucose below 70 mg/dL, level 2 is below 54 mg/dL, and level 3 is severe hypoglycemia that needs assistance from another person regardless of the number. Treat a conscious adult with 15 g of fast carbohydrate and recheck in 15 minutes.

Glucagon, 1 mg by injection or 3 mg intranasal, is the rescue drug when the patient cannot swallow. It works poorly when liver glycogen is gone, as in prolonged starvation or advanced liver disease. Give intravenous dextrose in that setting.

A supervised fast, up to 72 hours, is the test for insulinoma. End the fast when plasma glucose is below 55 mg/dL with symptoms. Endogenous hyperinsulinism at that point shows insulin at least 3 microunits/mL, C-peptide at least 0.6 ng/mL, and proinsulin at least 5 pmol/L, with a negative sulfonylurea screen.

Factitious insulin use causes hypoglycemia with a high insulin and a suppressed C-peptide. A sulfonylurea causes a high insulin and a high C-peptide, and the drug screen is positive. Both imitate insulinoma until the C-peptide and the screen are done.

Nonislet-cell tumor hypoglycemia is driven by incompletely processed IGF-2. Insulin, C-peptide, and IGF-1 are low, and a large mesenchymal or hepatic tumor is the usual source. Glucose must be given until the tumor is removed.

Impaired awareness of hypoglycemia follows recurrent lows and raises the risk of severe episodes. A period of 2 to 3 weeks with strict avoidance of glucose below 70 mg/dL can partly restore awareness. Automated insulin delivery is used when awareness is lost.

Post-bariatric hypoglycemia occurs one to three hours after a meal, with a high insulin from an exaggerated GLP-1 response. Diet is first-line, acarbose can blunt the glucose spike, and insulinoma is unlikely if the fasting glucose is normal.

topics.title: Chronic complications of diabetes
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 38 Complications of Diabetes Mellitus

mustKnow.fact: Screen for retinopathy at diagnosis in type 2 diabetes and within 5 years of diagnosis in type 1 diabetes, then at least yearly. Proliferative disease is defined by neovascularization. A rapid fall in HbA1c can worsen retinopathy in the short term, as seen with semaglutide in SUSTAIN-6, so existing retinopathy is checked before a large glucose drop.

Moderately increased albuminuria is a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30 to 299 mg/g, and severely increased albuminuria is 300 mg/g or higher. An ACE inhibitor or an ARB is used when albuminuria and hypertension coexist. Do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB.

Add an SGLT2 inhibitor for diabetic kidney disease with an eGFR in the range where the chosen drug has a kidney outcome, and consider finerenone when albuminuria persists on a renin-angiotensin blocker. Metformin is not kidney-protective therapy.

Distal symmetric polyneuropathy is the common neuropathy. Test with a 10 g monofilament yearly. Painful neuropathy is treated with pregabalin, duloxetine, or gabapentin. Tight glucose slows onset but rarely abolishes established pain.

Cardiac autonomic neuropathy causes resting tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, and a higher mortality. Gastroparesis causes early satiety and a mismatch between insulin and food. Metoclopramide is limited by tardive dyskinesia and is not a long-term casual prescription.

Charcot neuroarthropathy is a hot, swollen, relatively painless foot in a patient with neuropathy and intact pulses. Offload it in a total contact cast. Treating it as cellulitis alone and letting the patient walk destroys the arch.

The main biochemical routes of microvascular injury are the polyol pathway, advanced glycation end products, protein kinase C activation, and oxidative stress. They explain why glucose itself, not only blood pressure, drives retinopathy and nephropathy.

Steno-2 showed that targeting glucose, blood pressure, lipids, and smoking together reduces cardiovascular events and microvascular disease more than glucose control alone. A foot ulcer also needs vascular assessment, because an ankle-brachial index can be falsely high when arteries are calcified.

topics.title: Diabetes in pregnancy
topics.book: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology 15e Ch. 19 Endocrine Changes in Pregnancy; NICE diabetes in pregnancy; ADA Standards of Care 2025

mustKnow.fact: NICE diagnoses gestational diabetes when the fasting plasma glucose is at least 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) or the 2-hour value on a 75 g OGTT is at least 7.8 mmol/L (140 mg/dL). IADPSG, from the HAPO study, uses a 75 g OGTT and diagnoses diabetes if any one value is met: fasting 92, 1 hour 180, or 2 hour 153 mg/dL. The thresholds disagree. Where a single rule is required, NICE is the default named here, and IADPSG is the alternative international criteria.

DIPSI is the Indian programme test: a non-fasting 75 g load with a 2-hour glucose of 140 mg/dL or higher. It is labelled separately from NICE and from IADPSG because it does not use a fasting sample and it misses some women the other criteria would detect.

When diet does not control gestational diabetes, NICE allows metformin and adds insulin if metformin is unsuitable, declined, or not enough. The ADA prefers insulin and notes that metformin crosses the placenta. The disagreement is real; this blueprint follows NICE as the default and records the ADA position beside it.
